questions.q: Which serving pattern is described as the most common starting point for a single model needing a fast OpenAI-compatible API?
options: TensorRT-LLM compiled from scratch with no serving layer
vLLM alone
Triton hosting ten unrelated models
A custom-built HTTP server with no framework at all
questions.explain: vLLM alone is the most common starting point: it works with minimal setup and ships an OpenAI-compatible API out of the box, which covers many teams' needs without further tooling.

questions.q: When does compiling with TensorRT-LLM (behind Triton) tend to pay off?
options: Only for teams running on non-NVIDIA hardware
At high enough request volume that the throughput gain translates into meaningful GPU-cost savings, for teams committed to NVIDIA hardware
Only when serving exactly one request per day
Never — it has no advantages over vLLM
questions.explain: Compiling with TensorRT-LLM costs real setup and maintenance time, which is worth it once the throughput/latency gain is large enough at scale to justify that cost, and requires being committed to NVIDIA hardware.

questions.q: Why would an organization choose Triton specifically, over running vLLM or TensorRT-LLM standalone?
options: Because Triton is always the fastest option for any single model
Because it needs to serve many different kinds of models under one consistent operational surface (shared health checks, metrics, deployment process)
Because Triton eliminates the need for any GPU
Because Triton cannot host vLLM or TensorRT-LLM models at all
questions.explain: Triton's advantage shows up most clearly when an organization has model diversity and wants one consistent operational surface across many different model frameworks, rather than managing each separately.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is "which tool is fastest" the wrong first question to ask?
options: Because speed never matters in production
Because raw speed comparisons are highly dependent on the specific model, GPU, batch size, and workload, and can reverse under different conditions
Because all three tools always produce identical benchmark results
Because benchmarking is technically impossible
questions.explain: Benchmark results between these tools vary significantly by model, hardware, batch size, and request pattern, so a result favoring one tool under one workload may not hold under another — fit to constraints matters more than a single speed number.

questions.q: Which question is NOT listed in this lesson as something to ask before choosing a serving setup?
options: How many different models do we need to serve, and how similar are their frameworks?
How much engineering time can we spend on performance tuning versus shipping?
Are we committed to NVIDIA hardware, or do we need flexibility?
What programming language was the original research paper written in?
questions.explain: The lesson's four questions concern model diversity, available tuning time, hardware commitment, and API requirements — not the programming language of any research paper, which is irrelevant to the decision.
